sections.title: What happens when you type a URL

blocks.text: Before the first byte of the response, the user has paid for a DNS lookup and two round trips. At 150 ms RTT that's ~300 ms of pure network setup — which is why edges near users, connection reuse, and HTTP/3's faster handshakes matter more than shaving server milliseconds.

items: Records: A/AAAA (IP), CNAME (alias), MX, TXT; TTLs control caching.
**GeoDNS / latency-based routing:** return the IP of the nearest healthy region.
**Failover is slow:** resolvers and clients cache for the TTL (and some ignore low TTLs). Use anycast or a global load balancer for fast failover.
DNS is also a dependency that can fail — managed DNS providers are highly redundant for a reason.

cols.title: TCP
pros: What HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, databases, gRPC use
cons: Handshake cost; head-of-line blocking: one lost packet delays everything behind it

cols.title: UDP
pros: Ideal when late data is useless (voice, video, games)
cons: Apps handle loss/order themselves; often blocked by middleboxes

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: QUIC (HTTP/3) builds reliable, multiplexed streams on top of UDP, so a lost packet only stalls its own stream, and connections survive network changes (Wi-Fi → cellular).

items: Provides encryption, integrity and server authentication (certificates signed by a CA).
TLS 1.3 needs one round trip to set up (0-RTT for resumed sessions, with replay caveats).
Terminate TLS at the edge/load balancer to offload CPU and centralise certificates; re-encrypt to backends or use mTLS internally.

sections.title: Load balancing at layer 4 vs layer 7

head: L4
L7
rows: Fine, but balances per connection unless HTTP/2-aware

items: **HTTP/1.1:** one request at a time per connection; browsers open ~6 per host.
**HTTP/2:** many concurrent streams over one TCP connection, header compression, server push (deprecated). Default for gRPC.
**HTTP/3:** HTTP/2 semantics over QUIC/UDP; better on lossy mobile networks.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Putting an L4 balancer in front of gRPC services. HTTP/2 multiplexes all requests over one long-lived connection, so L4 balancing sends everything from a client to one backend. Use an L7 (HTTP/2-aware) proxy or client-side load balancing.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Clients hit the nearest edge via anycast; TLS terminates there; an L7 proxy routes by path to services over pooled HTTP/2 connections; WebSockets go through an L4 balancer to a gateway tier.
